docs.title: hone
docs.text: hone is a Python optimization engine. It finds the parameters that minimize or maximize a function you give it, and is built for functions that are slow, noisy or constrained: simulations, physical tests and model training.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install hone-python

It needs Python 3.12 or later. The package is named hone-python because hone is taken on PyPI; in code it is still import hone.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
from hone import GeneticOptimizer, GeneticOptimizerConfig, RangeParameter


def objective_function(x, y):
    return x**2 + y**2


# Each parameter of the objective function is declared with the values it may take.
x = RangeParameter("x", -5, 5)
y = RangeParameter("y", -5, 5)

optimizer = GeneticOptimizer(search_space=[x, y], config=GeneticOptimizerConfig(threshold=0.01, seed=0))
result = optimizer.optimize(objective_function)
print(result.best_fitness, result.best_params)

The optimizer minimizes by default; set maximize=True in the config to maximize instead.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • A documentation site, at https://hone-python.dev/, built with MkDocs Material. Its guide, examples, benchmark results and changelog are pulled from the README, the example scripts and the benchmark files, so each is still written once, and its API reference is generated from the docstrings. Every config field now has a docstring, which also becomes its description in the config's JSON schema. CI builds the site on every pull request and publishes it on every push to main; see "Docs" in the README.

docs.title: Internal
docs.text: • CI is hardened against supply-chain attacks. Every workflow is read-only unless a job needs more, every action is pinned by commit, and checkouts don't keep the token. Poetry is installed from a hash-pinned requirements file, and the Docker image's base is pinned by digest and runs the tests as an ordinary user. Released packages carry a build provenance attestation, which gh attestation verify checks, alongside PyPI's own. Pull requests are checked for dependencies with known vulnerabilities, zizmor lints the workflows, and OpenSSF Scorecard scores the repository weekly. Dependabot keeps actions, dependencies, Poetry and the base image current.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • A security policy, SECURITY.md: how to report a vulnerability privately through GitHub, which versions get fixes (the latest minor release), and what counts. Running your own objective and constraint functions and loading pickled checkpoints are by design; running code or touching files when loading a result or a config is a vulnerability. The README links to it.

Several objectives at once: a run returns the front of best trade-offs rather than one answer to a weighted score, and the choice between them is made after seeing what each costs. NSGA2 searches for the front on larger budgets and multi-objective Bayesian optimization on small ones, choose_pareto_optimizer picks between them, and a multi-objective benchmark suite backs the choice. A README section explains them, and an example designs a beam that is light, cheap and stiff. See benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Several objectives at once. MultiObjectiveConfig(objectives={"accuracy": "maximize", "cost": "minimize"}) names each objective, and the objective function returns a dict of them. A run returns a ParetoResult whose front holds the best trade-offs among everything evaluated: front.best("accuracy", where={"cost": 20}) is the most accurate design costing at most 20, front.closest() the most balanced by augmented Chebyshev distance on the front's own scale, and front.hypervolume(reference) scores the front. With noise, each point on the front is an average and comes with its standard error. A dict with the wrong keys raises TypeError. MultiObjectiveRandomSearch is the baseline, and print_progress prints the size of the front and its hypervolume. See docs/design/multiple-objectives.md.
  • NSGA2, a genetic algorithm that searches for the front: it ranks the population by fronts and spreads it along them by crowding distance, and breeds with the genetic optimizer's crossover, mutation, constraint repair and niches, so it supports every kind of parameter, constraints and conditions. At 1,000 evaluations per dimension its median hypervolume gap is about 0.001 on the ZDT problems, ten times closer than weighted sums.
  • MultiObjectiveBayesian, for budgets of a few hundred evaluations or fewer. Each candidate draws random weights for the objectives and goes where a Gaussian process expects the most improvement in their augmented Chebyshev combination. method="parego", the default, models the combination; method="models" models each objective, which did better on the three-objective problem. At 10 evaluations per dimension ParEGO has the lowest gap on every problem any optimizer reaches.
  • choose_pareto_optimizer picks MultiObjectiveBayesian up to 200 evaluations and NSGA2 beyond, as the benchmark suggests.
  • A multi-objective benchmark suite. python -m hone.benchmarks --multi runs ZDT1 (also rotated), ZDT2, ZDT3, ZDT4, DTLZ2 and the welded beam's cost against its deflection, scored by hypervolume gap from the true front, against weighted sums of the objectives as the baseline. The summaries include each run's median attainment surface. See benchmarks/README.md.
  • An example, examples/cantilever_beam.py, designing a cantilever beam in steel, aluminium or carbon fibre against its mass, cost and deflection, under a stress limit that depends on the material, and choosing from the front.

docs.title: Internal
docs.text: • The optimizer base class is split into OptimizerCore, the generation loop, ask and tell, workers, checkpoints and run records shared by every optimizer, and Optimizer, which adds what a single objective needs. This makes room for multiple objectives (see docs/design/multiple-objectives.md). Results don't change, and checkpoints saved by 0.11.0 still load.

Conditional parameters: parameters that exist only while others take certain values, written model["svm"] >> [kernel, C], which every optimizer supports. A README section explains them, an example chooses a classifier and its settings in one search, and the benchmark has a conditional suite comparing each optimizer with searching every parameter all the time. See benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Conditional parameters. SearchSpace(parameters, conditions=[model["svm"] >> [kernel, C], kernel["rbf"] >> gamma]) switches parameters on only while a test holds: a choice parameter's values, such as model["svm"], or a comparison of range parameters in brackets, such as (layers >= 3) >> units_3. A parameter that is switched off isn't passed to the objective, which gives it a default, and results and initial points leave it out. Constraints on it apply only while it is switched on, and test >> constraint makes a constraint apply only while the test holds. Every optimizer supports them. See docs/design/conditions.md.
  • Bayesian optimization encodes a parameter switched off the same whatever value it holds, so its model isn't misled by values that don't matter. On the conditional benchmark its geometric-mean error is ×0.0004 and ×0.0003 that of the same problems with every parameter always on, at 10 and 20 evaluations per dimension.
  • The genetic optimizer keeps a value for every gene, switched off or not, takes a gene from the parent it is on in, and mutates only genes switched on. With conditions, niche_share defaults to 0.5, so each branch breeds within itself; its error is ×0.05, ×0.08 and ×0.00004 the always-on version's at 50, 100 and 1,000 evaluations per dimension.
  • CMA-ES searches conditions on range parameters, keeping a parameter's place in its distribution while it is switched off.
  • A conditional benchmark suite. python -m hone.benchmarks --conditional runs four problems with conditional parameters, each also as a flat version with every parameter always on, to compare. The machine learning suite gains model-selection-breast-cancer, which chooses a classifier and its settings, and its flat version.
  • An example, examples/choose_a_model.py, choosing among an SVM with three kernels, a random forest and logistic regression, with each one's settings and a conditional constraint on the forest's size.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • GeneticOptimizerConfig.niche_share defaults to None: 0.5 for a search space with conditions, and 0, as before, otherwise. Results without conditions don't change.

Constraints: limits across parameters, written with the parameters themselves, which every optimizer keeps to. A README section explains them, two examples work through a standard engineering design and a maintenance schedule, and the benchmark has a constrained suite. See benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Constraints. SearchSpace(parameters, constraints=[width * height <= 40, width >= 2 * height]) limits the search to points that satisfy every constraint, and the objective is never evaluated outside them. Constraints are written with range parameters and numbers, using +, -, *, /, ** and abs(), compared with <= or >=. Constraint.function(...) covers anything else, such as choice parameters; it isn't saved with a result, so rebuild_optimizer(functions=...) takes it again. Initial points must satisfy the constraints, and constraints that leave nothing to search raise InfeasibleSearchSpace before any evaluation. Every optimizer supports them: random search and Bayesian optimization only consider feasible points, CMA-ES draws a candidate again while it breaks a constraint, and the genetic optimizer moves an infeasible child back toward its fitter parent until it is feasible, near the boundary. python -m hone.benchmarks --constrained runs ten constrained problems, among them the pressure vessel, tension spring and welded beam design problems.
  • Two worked examples. examples/pressure_vessel.py designs a pressure vessel of least cost under three constraints, with integer plate thicknesses, and finds the best published design. examples/maintenance_schedule.py chooses a production line's maintenance schedule, scored by a noisy simulation of a year, under a limit on technician hours and one on planned stops that depends on the chosen shift.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Checkpoints no longer store the search space, which the optimizer loading one already has.

The genetic optimizer, retuned: adaptive mutation, no repeat evaluations and blend crossover. Against 0.8.2, its geometric-mean error on the benchmark's 36 problems falls to ×0.58, ×0.23, ×0.16, ×0.17 and ×0.012 at 10, 20, 50, 100 and 1,000 evaluations per dimension. Results of existing genetic optimizer runs change. Benchmark results are in benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The genetic optimizer adapts its mutation. Each individual carries its own mutation size, which its children inherit and vary, so selection tunes it as the run goes (adaptive_mutation, on by default). The default mutation_rate is now 1 over the number of variables, at least 0.1, rather than 0.1. On the benchmark's 36 problems the genetic optimizer's geometric-mean error falls to ×0.92, ×0.44, ×0.34, ×0.50 and ×0.33 at 10 to 1,000 evaluations per dimension, and it loses to random search on 14 problem and budget pairs rather than 37. With noise=True both stay as before, where they didn't help at large budgets. Results of existing runs change.
  • The genetic optimizer doesn't repeat evaluations. Without noise, a child that would repeat a point already asked for, such as a copy of a parent that no mutation touched, is mutated again until it is new. About one child in four used to be such a copy. The geometric-mean error falls to ×0.90, ×0.82, ×0.91, ×0.89 and ×0.41 at 10 to 1,000 evaluations per dimension. This happens even with mutation_rate=0. With noise=True repeats stay, since they refine a point's average. Results of existing runs change.
  • The genetic optimizer blends its children's numbers. Each range value of a child is drawn from between its parents' values, and up to blend_alpha (default 0.1) times their distance beyond, rather than copied from one parent (blend_crossover, on by default, with noise too). The geometric-mean error falls to ×0.69, ×0.62, ×0.51, ×0.38 and ×0.08 at 10 to 1,000 evaluations per dimension, and it loses to random search on 3 problem and budget pairs rather than 14. Results of existing runs change.
  • choose_optimizer sends problems with integer parameters to the genetic optimizer above 200 evaluations, rather than CMA-ES, since with blend crossover it does better on them. Its pick's error on the benchmark is ×1.37 the best optimizer's, against ×1.62 had integers stayed with CMA-ES.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: • Releases go to PyPI. Each new version is published as hone-python when it is released on GitHub, so pip install hone-python installs the latest release. This is the first.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Elites could fill the whole population. An elitism_rate below 1 could round to every individual, leaving nothing to evaluate, so the genetic optimizer stopped long before its budget was spent. At least one child is now bred each generation.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Noisy runs stopped early at the threshold on a lucky value. With noise=True, the threshold was checked against the best point's average as it stood when that point was first reported, not its current average. One lucky evaluation could end the run with reached_threshold set while the reported best_fitness had not reached threshold. The check now uses the reported best.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Property-based tests. pbt/tests/ checks the properties hone's documentation claims, using Hypothesis on generated search spaces and settings, and runs with the rest of the tests. pbt/SUMMARY.md lists them. Hypothesis is a new dev dependency.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Choosing an optimizer automatically. choose_optimizer(search_space, max_evaluations, ...) returns the optimizer the benchmark suggests: Bayesian optimization for 200 evaluations or fewer, then the genetic optimizer if there are choice parameters, and CMA-ES otherwise. On the benchmark, its pick's median error is 1.24 times the best optimizer's on geometric mean, against 5.9 times for always using CMA-ES.
  • Checkpoints. optimize(checkpoint="run.checkpoint") saves the run's state after each generation, and carries the run on from the file if it exists, so a killed run picks up where it left off with the same result as an uninterrupted one. save_checkpoint() and load_checkpoint() do the same for ask and tell.
  • Not waiting for the slowest evaluations. min_finished (default 1) is the share of each generation's evaluations that must finish before the next generation is bred. Below 1, slow evaluations finish in the background and their results join the generation under way, so workers no longer sit idle while one slow evaluation runs on. Bayesian optimization assumes evaluations still running come out as its model predicts, so it doesn't propose them again.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• A record of each run. Result.run holds how the result was produced: the optimizer, its full config including the seed, the search space, any initial points, the objective's name, workers and timeout, the versions of hone, Python and numpy, and when the run started and how long it took.
  • Rebuilding an optimizer from a result. result.rebuild_optimizer() sets up a new optimizer exactly as the result's was, so a saved run can be repeated.
  • Progress callbacks. optimize(callback=...) is called after each generation with a Progress. Return True to stop the run. print_progress prints a line per generation.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Ctrl+C returns the best result so far rather than discarding the run. optimize() stops its workers and returns the result with stopped set. If no evaluation has succeeded yet, Ctrl+C still raises KeyboardInterrupt.
  • Result equality compares what was found, not the new run record, so two runs with the same seed still compare equal.
  • Worker processes ignore Ctrl+C; the main process stops them.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Type information. hone ships a py.typed marker, so type checkers and editors use its type hints in your code. CI checks hone's own types with mypy.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• SearchSpace accepts any sequence of parameters, such as a tuple, not only a list.
  • Trial, the candidate ask() hands out, is a pydantic model like the rest of hone's data, so trial.model_dump() gives it as a dict. Its fields are unchanged.
New optimizers and parameter types, noise handling, time limits, and fixes from an expert review of 0.5.0. Benchmark results are in benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Bayesian optimization. BayesianOptimizer models the objective with a Gaussian process and evaluates where it expects the most improvement. It is the best optimizer in the benchmark when evaluations are scarce: at 10 and 20 evaluations per dimension it has the lowest median error on 30 and 31 of the 36 problems. It supports range and choice parameters, but not choose_n.
  • Log-scale ranges. RangeParameter(..., log=True) searches a range evenly in its logarithm, for settings that span orders of magnitude such as learning rates. It needs a positive minimum and works with integer=True.
  • Noisy objectives. noise=True averages every evaluation of the same point, and each optimizer uses the averages. final_evaluations (off by default) keeps evaluations back to re-evaluate the most promising points at the end.
  • Starting points. Every optimizer takes initial_points, such as a known good design or an earlier run's best parameters.
  • Time limits. optimize(timeout=...) stops any evaluation that runs longer than that many seconds and counts it as failed. Evaluations now run in hone's own pool of worker processes, so a hung or crashed evaluation is replaced instead of stalling the run.
  • Niches for the genetic optimizer. niche_share (off by default) breeds part of each generation within groups of parents that share the same choice parameter values. Set it to 0.5 when the best option of a choice parameter may be found late: on material-selection-10d it finds the right material in 10 of 10 runs, against 4 of 10 without.
  • Benchmarks.
  • Every problem runs at five budgets, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 1,000 evaluations per dimension.
  • Rotated versions of four test functions, in which the variables interact: 36 problems in all.
  • --ml tunes three scikit-learn models by cross-validation, and --noisy adds noise to six problems.
  • --jobs shares the runs among processes.
  • An example, examples/tune_iris.py, tuning a model on the Iris dataset.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
These change the results of existing code:

  • The genetic optimizer sizes its population from its budget. With max_evaluations set and no population_size, the population is about a twentieth of the budget, between 16 and 50, and the run continues until the budget is spent. Without a budget the defaults are unchanged.
  • Tournaments pick their best entrant. tournament_p now defaults to 1.0 rather than 0.75. The genetic optimizer's error falls by 11% to 64% across the benchmark's budgets.
  • CMA-ES with workers. Unless population_size is set, optimize(workers=n) gives CMA-ES at least 2n candidates per generation, so its results depend on the number of workers as well as the seed.
  • Infinite values count as failed evaluations, as NaN already did, and tell() rejects booleans.
  • An exception from the objective stops every worker at once, rather than waiting for the evaluations already running.
  • Benchmark command line. --budget-per-dimension is replaced by --budgets, and run_benchmark takes budgets_per_dimension.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• CMA-ES widened the steps of integer variables before learning from them, which inflated its step size on problems with integers. It now learns from the steps as drawn, as CMA-ES with Margin does.
  • With the spawn and forkserver start methods, the default from Python 3.14, the time limit counted each worker's start-up, so on slow machines every evaluation could time out.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: • The package is named hone-python, because hone is taken on PyPI: pip install hone-python. It still imports as hone.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: • scipy and threadpoolctl are now required. scikit-learn is needed only for the machine learning benchmark.

A rewrite of the 2023 version.

  • Parameters and configs are validated pydantic models: RangeParameter, ChoiceParameter and FixedParameter replace Constraint.
  • Every optimizer shares a base class with an ask/tell interface, parallel workers, failed evaluations, an exact max_evaluations budget, seeds and a savable Result.
  • CMA-ES, alongside the genetic optimizer and random search.
  • Fixes to the genetic optimizer's loop, selection, mutation and result.
  • A benchmark suite with a regression check in CI.
  • Python 3.12 or later; licensed under BSD-3-Clause.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: hone.benchmarks runs optimizers on test problems with known optima. See Benchmarks for what the suites measure and the latest results.

docs.title: run_benchmark
docs.text:
run_benchmark(problems: Iterable[Problem], optimizers: dict[str, OptimizerFactory] | None = None, seeds: Iterable[int] = range(10), budgets_per_dimension: Iterable[int] = BUDGETS, jobs: int = 1) -> list[Run]

Run every optimizer on every problem with every seed and every budget.

A budget of b evaluations per dimension gives a run b × dimensions evaluations. Each budget is a separate run, so an optimizer can choose its settings from the budget. An optimizer that cannot search a problem's parameters is skipped for that problem, and one whose factory raises SkipBudget is skipped at that budget. With jobs > 1, runs are shared among that many processes where the platform can fork them; the results are the same.

docs.text: Every optimizer takes a search space, a config and optional starting points, and supports optimize(), ask() and tell(). See Choosing an optimizer for which to use.

docs.title: choose_optimizer
docs.text:
choose_optimizer(search_space: SearchSpace | list[Parameter], max_evaluations: int, *, initial_points: dict[str, Any] | list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None, **config: Any) -> Optimizer

The optimizer the benchmark suggests for this search space and budget, set up to use it.

  • Up to 200 evaluations: Bayesian optimization, unless a choice parameter has choose_n.
  • More, with choice parameters: the genetic optimizer, since CMA-ES searches numbers only.
  • More, with integer parameters: the genetic optimizer, which did better on the benchmark's integer and mixed problems.
  • More, with continuous numbers only: CMA-ES.

Other settings, such as seed, maximize, noise or threshold, are passed on to the chosen optimizer's config. The optimizer's class and config show what was chosen.

docs.text:
BayesianOptimizer(search_space: SearchSpace | List[Parameter], config: BayesianConfig | None = None, *, initial_points: dict[str, Any] | list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None)

Bases: Optimizer, _ModelSearch

Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian process and expected improvement.

The first generation is spread over the search space (with any initial points). After that, each candidate is the point where a Gaussian process model of the objective predicts the largest expected improvement on the best value so far. Failed evaluations are modelled as the worst value seen, which steers the search away from them.

Range parameters, integer or not, and choice parameters are supported, but not choice parameters with choose_n. Fixed parameters are passed through.

load_checkpoint(path: str | Path) -> None

Carry on the run saved in path by save_checkpoint(), from where it was saved.

The checkpoint must come from an optimizer set up like this one: the same class, config, search space and initial points. Trials handed out but not yet told when it was saved are handed out again by ask(), and can still be told by their ids.

A checkpoint is a pickle, which can run code when it is loaded: only load checkpoints you saved yourself.

docs.title: optimize
docs.text:
optimize(objective_function: Callable, *, workers: int = 1, timeout: float | None = None, callback: Callable[[Any], bool | None] | None = None, checkpoint: str | Path | None = None) -> ResultT

Run the optimizer from the start, calling objective_function for every candidate.

The function is called with one keyword argument per parameter. To record an evaluation as failed, raise EvaluationFailed or return NaN or infinity; any other exception stops the run. With a seed, every call with the same number of workers returns the same result. The genetic optimizer and random search return it however many workers are used; CMA-ES and Bayesian optimization do not, because their default population grows with the number of workers.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default objective_function Callable

The function to optimize.

required workers int

Evaluate candidates in this many background processes at once.

1 timeout float | None

The longest, in seconds, one evaluation may take. An evaluation that runs longer is stopped and counts as failed, as does one whose process crashes.

None callback Callable[[Any], bool | None] | None

Called with the progress after each generation. Return True from it to stop the run; optimize() then returns the result so far.

None checkpoint str | Path | None

A file to save the run's state to after each generation. If the file exists, the run carries on from it instead of starting over, so a run killed partway through picks up where it left off; one that finished returns its result at once. The result is the same as an uninterrupted run's.

None

Pressing Ctrl+C also stops the run and returns the result so far, marked as stopped, once at least one evaluation has succeeded.

With workers > 1 or a timeout, each evaluation runs in a separate process, so the function must be defined at the top level of a module.

CMAES(search_space: SearchSpace | List[Parameter], config: CMAESConfig | None = None, *, initial_points: dict[str, Any] | list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None)

Bases: Optimizer

Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, for range parameters.

Each generation samples candidates from a multivariate normal distribution, then moves the distribution's centre toward the best of them and reshapes it to stretch along the directions that improved. It learns the scale of each variable and how variables interact, which makes it strong on smooth continuous problems.

Range parameters, continuous or integer, are searched; fixed parameters are passed through. Choice parameters are not supported: use GeneticOptimizer for those. A range a condition switches off keeps its place in the distribution; its value is ignored.

The search starts at the centre of every range. With initial points, it evaluates them first and starts at the best one instead; a smaller initial_step then keeps the search close to it.

docs.title: GeneticOptimizer
docs.text:
GeneticOptimizer(search_space: SearchSpace | List[Parameter], config: OptimizerConfig | None = None, *, initial_points: dict[str, Any] | list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None)

Bases: Optimizer, Breeding

Function optimizer that employs an implementation of the genetic algorithm. The genetic algorithm is a metaheuristic inspired by the process of natural selection. It is a population-based algorithm that uses the concepts of selection, crossover, and mutation to evolve a population of individuals towards a solution to the objective function.

The first generation is any initial points, then random candidates. Each later generation keeps the previous one's elites unchanged, then fills the rest of the population with children: two parents are selected, crossed over, and mutated. Failed evaluations are never elites or parents.

With blend crossover, each range value of a child is drawn from between its parents' values, and a little beyond, rather than copied from one of them; choices and fixed values are still copied.

With adaptive mutation, each individual carries its own mutation size, as in evolution strategies: a child takes the geometric mean of its parents' sizes, varied at random, so individuals with sizes that suit the problem's current scale breed more.

Without noise, a child that repeats a point already asked for, such as a copy of a parent that no mutation touched, has one gene at a time mutated again until it is new, since evaluating it again would only spend the budget. With noise, repeats stay: they refine the point's average.

With conditional parameters, every individual keeps a value for each parameter, even one switched off at its point, so a child that switches a branch back on inherits settings that once did well there. A gene switched off in one parent but on in the other comes from the parent it is on in, and only genes switched on are mutated.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default search_space SearchSpace | List[Parameter]

The parameters to optimize over, as a SearchSpace or a list of parameters.

required config OptimizerConfig | None

A GeneticOptimizerConfig. Defaults are used if omitted.

None

Example:

>>> from hone import GeneticOptimizer, GeneticOptimizerConfig, RangeParameter
>>>
>>> def objective_function(x, y):
>>>     return x**2 + y**2
>>>
>>> x = RangeParameter("x", -5, 5)
>>> y = RangeParameter("y", -5, 5)
>>>
>>> optimizer = GeneticOptimizer(search_space=[x, y], config=GeneticOptimizerConfig(threshold=0.01))
>>> result = optimizer.optimize(objective_function)

docs.text:
MultiObjectiveBayesian(search_space: SearchSpace | List[Parameter], config: MultiObjectiveBayesianConfig | None = None, *, initial_points: dict[str, Any] | list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None)

Bases: MultiObjectiveOptimizer, _ModelSearch

Bayesian optimization for several objectives, returning the front of best trade-offs.

The first generation is spread over the search space, as in BayesianOptimizer. Each later candidate aims at a different part of the front: it draws random weights for the objectives, each scaled by the range seen so far, and goes where the model expects the most improvement in their augmented Chebyshev combination, the largest weighted gap from the best values plus a twentieth of their sum. Unlike a weighted sum, this reaches every part of the front, including any dent in it. With method "parego" one Gaussian process models the combination (ParEGO, Knowles 2006); with "models" one models each objective, and the combination is applied to their predictions.

Range and choice parameters are supported, as in BayesianOptimizer, with constraints and conditions. Each candidate takes a fraction of a second or more to choose, so it suits expensive objectives and budgets of a few hundred evaluations.

docs.text:
NSGA2(search_space: SearchSpace | List[Parameter], config: OptimizerConfig | None = None, *, initial_points: dict[str, Any] | list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None)

Bases: MultiObjectiveOptimizer, Breeding

The genetic optimizer for several objectives, returning the front of best trade-offs.

Each generation, the previous generation and its children are sorted into fronts: the points nothing dominates, then those only the first front dominates, and so on. The best fronts survive, and where one doesn't fit whole, its most isolated points do, by crowding distance, so the front stays spread out. Parents are chosen from the survivors by tournaments of two, won by the better front and then the more isolated point. Children are bred as in the genetic optimizer, with its crossover, mutation, repeat avoidance, repair for constraints, conditions and niches.

The result's front is that of every point evaluated, not only the survivors, so a trade-off found early is never lost when crowding drops it from the population. Ties are broken by the order points were created, so a seeded run repeats exactly, and its result doesn't depend on the number of workers.

Bases: OptimizerCore[ParetoResult]

Base class for optimizers of several objectives, which return a ParetoResult.

The objective function returns a dict with one value per objective named in the config's objectives, such as {"accuracy": 0.97, "cost": 12.0}, and tell() takes the same. A dict with missing or extra keys, or a value that isn't a number, raises TypeError: it is a bug in the objective. Raise EvaluationFailed, or return NaN or infinity for any objective, to record an evaluation as failed; failed evaluations are never on the front.

The front is that of every point evaluated, not only the latest generation, so a trade-off found early is never lost. With noise, each point's values are the averages of all its evaluations, and the front comes with their standard errors.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
hone.benchmarks runs optimizers on test problems with known optima and reports how close each one gets:

python -m hone.benchmarks                  # full suite: 36 problems, 10 seeds each, five budgets
python -m hone.benchmarks --quick          # 6 problems, 5 seeds, three budgets; takes seconds
python -m hone.benchmarks --budgets 10 20  # only the budgets you name, in evaluations per dimension
python -m hone.benchmarks --multi          # several objectives: 7 problems, scored by hypervolume gap

The suite has five standard continuous functions (sphere, ellipsoid, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin and Ackley) in 2, 5 and 10 dimensions, rotated versions of four of them in which the variables interact, and integer, mixed and categorical problems: 36 in all. Each function is shifted so its optimum is away from the centre of the search space. Every optimizer gets exactly the same number of evaluations. Each problem runs at five budgets, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 1,000 evaluations per dimension, because the best optimizer for a slow simulation that allows a few dozen runs is often not the best one for a cheap function evaluated thousands of times. Latest results are in benchmarks/results.md.

To compare your own optimizer, pass a factory that builds it for a problem, a budget and a seed. The budget is the run's total number of evaluations, so the factory can choose settings to suit it:

from hone.benchmarks import run_benchmark, standard_problems, summarize, to_markdown

runs = run_benchmark(standard_problems(), optimizers={"mine": make_my_optimizer})
print(to_markdown(summarize(runs)))

docs.title: Machine learning tuning
docs.text:
python -m hone.benchmarks --ml (or make benchmark-ml) tunes real models, each scored by 5-fold cross-validation on a dataset bundled with scikit-learn, which these problems need (pip install scikit-learn):

Problem Model and data Searched svm-breast-cancer Support vector classifier, 569 breast tumour samples C and gamma kernel-ridge-diabetes Kernel ridge regression of disease progression, 442 patients alpha, gamma and the kernel random-forest-wine 20-tree random forest, 178 wines in 3 classes depth, leaf size, features per split and split criterion

The best possible score is unknown, so error is measured from the best score a long reference search found. They run at 10, 20 and 50 evaluations per dimension, the budgets model tuning usually has. Results are in benchmarks/ml-results.md.

examples/tune_iris.py shows the same kind of tuning in a few lines. C and gamma span orders of magnitude, so they are log-scale ranges:

def accuracy(C, gamma, kernel):
    model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(C=C, gamma=gamma, kernel=kernel))
    return cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=folds).mean()

search_space = [
    RangeParameter("C", 1e-3, 1e3, log=True),
    RangeParameter("gamma", 1e-4, 10, log=True),
    ChoiceParameter("kernel", ["rbf", "sigmoid"]),
]
result = BayesianOptimizer(search_space, BayesianConfig(max_evaluations=30, maximize=True)).optimize(accuracy)

This folder holds the results of python -m hone.benchmarks:

File Contents results.md The full suite's results table, from make benchmark full-summaries.json The same results as data noisy-results.md The noisy problems' results, from make benchmark-noisy noisy-summaries.json The same results as data ml-results.md The machine learning tuning results, from make benchmark-ml ml-summaries.json The same results as data constrained-results.md The constrained problems' results, from make benchmark-constrained constrained-summaries.json The same results as data conditional-results.md The conditional problems' results, from make benchmark-conditional conditional-summaries.json The same results as data multi-results.md The multi-objective problems' results, from make benchmark-multi multi-summaries.json The same results as data, with each run's median attainment surface quick-baseline.json The quick suite's results, which CI compares every change against

docs.title: What the suite measures
docs.text:
Each optimizer runs on each problem with 10 seeds at five budgets: 10, 20, 50, 100 and 1,000 evaluations per dimension, so a 5-dimensional problem gets 50, 100, 250, 500 and 5,000 evaluations. Each budget is a separate run. The small budgets stand for expensive evaluations, such as a simulation that takes minutes, where a few dozen runs may be all there is time for. At every budget all optimizers get exactly the same number of evaluations.

The results start with an overview: for each budget, the number of problems on which each optimizer has the lowest median error. A table per budget follows, reporting the median error, the best value found minus the problem's known optimum, and the share of runs solved to an error of 0.0001 or less.

Every variable lies in [-5, 5]. Each problem is shifted so its optimum sits at a fixed point away from the centre, so an optimizer that drifts toward the centre gains nothing.

The plain functions are separable: each variable affects the value on its own, so an optimizer can improve one variable at a time. Engineering problems rarely behave like that, so ellipsoid, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin and Ackley also appear rotated, which mixes the variables together. Sphere is the same under any rotation and appears only once.

Problem What it tests sphere Plain convergence on a smooth bowl ellipsoid Variables on very different scales: axis weights range from 1 to 1,000,000 rosenbrock Following a long, curved valley rastrigin Escaping a regular grid of local minima ackley Finding a narrow hole in an almost flat surface rotated-* The same functions turned by a fixed random rotation, so the variables interact rather than each acting on its own integer-sphere Integer variables only mixed-rastrigin Half continuous and half integer variables material-selection A categorical choice that moves where the best continuous design is. Each material adds a base cost; titanium, at cost 0, gives the optimum

docs.title: At small budgets
docs.text:
• Bayesian optimization is the best optimizer when evaluations are scarce. At 10 and 20 evaluations per dimension it has the lowest median error on 29 and 30 of the 36 problems, and it beats CMA-ES on 28 and 29 of the 33 they share. On sphere-10d with 100 evaluations its median error is 0.0058, against 8.5 for CMA-ES; on ellipsoid-10d it is 666 against 235,000. It is also the only optimizer that reliably picks the right material at small budgets: on material-selection-5d at 20 evaluations per dimension its median error is 0.00066, against 1.7 for the genetic optimizer. Its losses are mostly rotated Rosenbrock, a long curved valley its model struggles to follow, and Rastrigin in 2 dimensions.
  • It runs only up to 200 evaluations. Each candidate costs a model fit and a search over the model, so the benchmark leaves it out of larger budgets (marked n/a): in the full suite it runs at 50 evaluations per dimension only on the 2-dimensional problems, and not at 100 or 1,000.
  • Without Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES would be the best at every small budget. With 50 evaluations per dimension on sphere-10d its median error is 0.0245, against 0.10 for the genetic optimizer and 21.8 for random search.
  • The genetic optimizer sizes its population from the budget. With a fixed population of 50, a budget of 50 evaluations or fewer ran out during its first, random generation, so it was exactly random search on every problem with 5 dimensions or fewer. It now uses about a twentieth of the budget, between 16 and 50. Against the fixed population, its geometric-mean error falls by 8% at 10 evaluations per dimension, 16% at 20, 28% at 50 and 12% at 100, and is unchanged at 1,000. With the tournament fix, adaptive mutation, repeat avoidance and blend crossover below, it beats random search on 33 problems at 10 evaluations per dimension and all 36 at 50, up from 9 and 29 before these changes.
  • Tournaments now always pick their best entrant. They used to pick the worst of the four 25% of the time (tournament_p=0.75), which slowed the search for nothing. With tournament_p=1.0 the genetic optimizer's geometric-mean error falls by 11% at 10 evaluations per dimension, 17% at 20, 64% at 50, 21% at 100 and 24% at 1,000, and it improves on 22 to 28 of the 36 problems at each budget. Tournament sizes of 2, 3, 6 and 8 were also tried; 4 stays.
  • Mutation adapts as the run goes. Each individual carries its own mutation size, which its children inherit and vary, so selection tunes it to the problem's current scale; and each value mutates with probability 1 over the number of variables, at least 0.1, rather than always 0.1. The genetic optimizer's geometric-mean error falls to ×0.92 at 10 evaluations per dimension, ×0.44 at 20, ×0.34 at 50, ×0.50 at 100 and ×0.33 at 1,000. It used to lose to random search on 37 problem and budget pairs, mostly badly scaled ones its fixed step couldn't follow; it now loses on 14, and on none at 1,000 evaluations per dimension. ellipsoid-2d at 50 evaluations per dimension falls from 11,600 to 74, against 867 for random search. Changing the step from the parents' spread instead, or letting it adapt faster, did worse. With noise=True both changes are off, because on the noisy problems they cost more at 200 evaluations per dimension than they gained at small budgets; noisy results are unchanged.
  • Children no longer repeat points already evaluated. About one child in four used to be an exact copy of a point already asked for, most often a parent that no mutation touched, and evaluating it again only spent the budget. Such a child is now mutated again, one value at a time, until it is new. The genetic optimizer's geometric-mean error falls to ×0.90 at 10 evaluations per dimension, ×0.82 at 20, ×0.91 at 50, ×0.89 at 100 and ×0.41 at 1,000, and every problem family improves. Doubling the mutation size on each retry changed nothing measurable. With noise=True repeats stay, because they refine a point's average; noisy results are unchanged.
  • Children's numbers are blended from their parents'. Uniform crossover copied each number from one parent or the other, so a child could only recombine values the population already had. Blend crossover draws each range value from between the two parents' values, and up to a tenth of their distance beyond either. The genetic optimizer's geometric-mean error falls to ×0.69 at 10 evaluations per dimension, ×0.62 at 20, ×0.51 at 50, ×0.38 at 100 and ×0.08 at 1,000; it is better on 136 problem and budget pairs and worse on 17, and loses to random search on 3 rather than 14. Widths of 0, 0.05 and 0.2 did about as well as 0.1; 0.3 and 0.5 did worse. With blend crossover, mutation sizes stop shrinking, since crossover does the fine convergence, but adaptive mutation still earns its place: without it the error at 1,000 evaluations per dimension is 2.3 times higher. Blend crossover also stays on with noise=True, where it helped (×0.67, ×0.84 and ×0.99 on the noisy problems).
  • Categorical problems have no strong option yet. CMA-ES can't run them. The genetic optimizer still often settles on the wrong material: its median error on material-selection-10d at 50 evaluations per dimension is 2.1. The opt-in niches below fix that on larger budgets.

docs.title: At 1,000 evaluations per dimension
docs.text:
CMA-ES runs on the 33 problems without choice parameters. Against the genetic optimizer it wins 24, ties 4 (the integer spheres and mixed-rastrigin-2d, which both solve) and loses 5: plain Rastrigin and plain mixed Rastrigin in 5 and 10 dimensions, and rotated Rastrigin in 2.

  • Most of those wins come from separability. Uniform crossover takes each variable from one parent or the other, which works well when variables act independently. Rotated, the genetic optimizer's median error on Rastrigin rises from 0.0014 to 9.5 in 10 dimensions, nearly seven-thousandfold, while CMA-ES's barely changes (5.47 to 6.47). CMA-ES wins 11 of the 12 rotated problems.
  • Smooth and badly scaled problems: CMA-ES by far, rotated or not. It solves sphere, ellipsoid, Rosenbrock and Ackley to between about 1e-11 and 1e-17 in every dimension. On rotated-ellipsoid-10d the genetic optimizer's median error is 1,600.
  • Rastrigin stays hard for CMA-ES at this budget. Its deep, dense local minima trap it; solving it reliably takes much larger populations than 1,000 evaluations per dimension allows the restarts to reach.
  • Categorical problems: only the genetic optimizer. On material-selection-10d 6 of its 10 runs find titanium and solve it, but the other 4 settle on a wrong material with a base cost of 1 to 3. With niche_share=0.5, which breeds half of each generation within groups sharing the same material, all 10 runs find titanium. At 200 evaluations per dimension niches raise the runs that find titanium from 6 to 9 of 10, though the median error rises from 0.012 to 0.029, because tuning the numbers within each niche is slower. Niches cost a little on small budgets (material-selection-5d at 50 evaluations per dimension gets worse), so they are off by default, and they change nothing on problems without choice parameters.
  • The genetic optimizer against random search: it now beats or ties it on every problem. Before adaptive mutation it lost five, among them rosenbrock-2d and rotated-ellipsoid-2d, where its fixed mutation step was too coarse for the precision they need.

CMA-ES now widens the steps of integer variables only where they are sampled, and adapts from the unwidened steps, as CMA-ES with Margin does. Before, the widening also inflated the steps of the continuous variables in the same run. This changes nothing measurable on the full suite, where integer variables are few, but on a 10-dimensional problem with one integer variable it lets the continuous variables converge as they would without it.

Since 0.5.0 every optimizer gets exactly the same number of evaluations. Before, the genetic optimizer used about 10% fewer than its budget, because it does not evaluate its elites again.

docs.title: Choosing an optimizer automatically
docs.text:
choose_optimizer turns these results into a rule: Bayesian optimization for 200 evaluations or fewer, then the genetic optimizer if there are choice or integer parameters, and CMA-ES otherwise. Integer problems went to CMA-ES until blend crossover made the genetic optimizer better on them; sending them to it lowers the pick's error on the standard suite from ×1.62 to ×1.37. For each problem and budget, its pick's median error was compared with the best optimizer's:

Suite Pick's error against the best, geometric mean Best on Always CMA-ES Always the genetic optimizer Standard, 36 problems × 5 budgets ×1.37 146 of 180 ×7.9, and 15 it can't run ×39 Noisy, 6 × 3 ×1.07 12 of 18 ×1.69, and 3 it can't run ×1.58 Machine learning, 3 × 3 ×1.05 8 of 9 ×1.14, and 6 it can't run ×23 Constrained, 10 × 5 ×1.04 45 of 50 ×21 ×202

A test (tests/test_choose_optimizer.py) recomputes this from the saved summaries, so the rule stays backed by the results whenever they are regenerated. A rule that also limited Bayesian optimization to 50 evaluations per variable did worse (×1.36 on the standard suite), so the simpler one stays.

docs.title: Machine learning tuning
docs.text:
python -m hone.benchmarks --ml tunes three scikit-learn models by 5-fold cross-validation, at 10, 20 and 50 evaluations per dimension: a support vector classifier on breast cancer data (C and gamma), kernel ridge regression on diabetes data (alpha, gamma and the kernel), and a random forest on wine data (depth, leaf size, features per split and split criterion). A fourth, model-selection-breast-cancer, chooses one of three classifiers for the breast cancer data, a support vector classifier, a random forest or k nearest neighbours, and that model's settings, with conditions; model-selection-breast-cancer-flat is the same with every model's settings always searched. Each problem minimizes 1 − accuracy or 1 − R², so an error of 0.0035 on the breast cancer problem is 0.35 percentage points of accuracy, about 2 of its 569 samples.

The optimum of a real model is unknown, so error is measured from the best score of a reference search: Bayesian optimization with 200 evaluations, and CMA-ES (where it applies), the genetic optimizer and random search with 1,000 each, three seeds of each.

What the results show:

  • Bayesian optimization is the best tuner. At 20 and 50 evaluations per dimension it has the lowest median error on the three single-model problems, and at 20 on all five. On the kernel ridge problem it finds the reference R² in 60% of runs with 60 evaluations and in every run with 150, where no other optimizer gets within 0.0005 in its median run.
  • Conditions help model selection. With conditions, Bayesian optimization's median error is 0.0018, one sample of 569, at both 10 and 20 evaluations per dimension (90 and 180 evaluations), and it finds the reference score in 30% of runs; with every setting always searched it is 0.0053 and 0.0026, and it never finds it. The genetic optimizer's is 0.0026 against 0.0035 at 20 evaluations per dimension, and the same at 10 and 50. Every reference run chose the support vector classifier.
  • The differences are smaller than on the test functions. Most settings of a well-chosen model score within a percentage point or two of the best, so random search is a fair tuner, as the hyperparameter tuning literature also finds. The extra value of a better optimizer shows in the last fraction of a point, and in how few evaluations it takes to get there.
  • Scores move in steps. Accuracy changes in multiples of one sample, so several optimizers often stop at exactly the same score: the random forest's median error is 0.0057 for every optimizer at 10 evaluations per dimension.
  • The genetic optimizer is better than random search here, but not by much. It wins on kernel ridge at 10 and 20 evaluations per dimension and on the SVM at 20 and 50, ties on the SVM at 10 and on the random forest, and loses narrowly on kernel ridge at 50. Adaptive mutation cut its median error to ×0.74 to ×0.84; avoiding repeats changed it by ×1.15, ×0.84 and ×0.83, and blend crossover by ×0.91, ×0.97 and ×1.47, at 10, 20 and 50 evaluations per dimension. Both losses are on kernel ridge. With budgets of 20 to 200 evaluations it runs only a few generations.

docs.title: Conditional problems
docs.text:
python -m hone.benchmarks --conditional runs four problems with conditional parameters, at the same five budgets, each twice: with its conditions, and as a -flat version with every parameter always on and the function ignoring those it doesn't use. The flat version is how such a space was searched before conditions, so the pair shows what conditions are worth.

Problem What it tests branches-3x2d and branches-3x5d A choice of three branches, each with its own 2 or 5 numbers. The best is a steep, narrow bowl reaching 0; the decoys are a wide, shallow bowl with a floor of 1 and a shallow Rastrigin grid with a floor of 0.5, where random points score better nested-9 A choice of model, one with a choice of kernel, one kernel with numbers of its own: the best point is two conditions deep, past a wide decoy with a floor of 0.25 layers-7 A layer count from 1 to 5 whose larger values switch on more numbers; 3 layers is best. Its conditions test a range, so CMA-ES can search it

Geometric-mean error over the four problems, with conditions over the flat versions:

Optimizer 10 / dim 20 / dim 50 / dim 100 / dim 1,000 / dim Bayesian optimization ×0.0004 ×0.0003 not run not run not run Genetic optimizer ×1.04 ×0.86 ×0.05 ×0.08 ×0.00004 CMA-ES (layers-7 only) ×1 ×1 ×1 ×1 ×1 Random search ×1 ×1 ×1 ×1 ×1
  • Bayesian optimization gains the most. Points that differ only in a parameter switched off are the same point to its model, so the values those parameters happen to hold add no noise. On branches-3x2d at 10 evaluations per dimension its median error is 0.00001 with conditions, against 0.87 flat; on nested-9, 0.0006 against 0.48. It is the best optimizer on most problems at 10 and 20 evaluations per dimension.
  • The genetic optimizer gains from niches, which conditions turn on. Without niches it settled in a decoy branch on most problems, flat or not: a wide branch fills the population before the narrow best one is tuned. With conditions, niche_share defaults to 0.5, so each branch breeds within itself, and at 1,000 evaluations per dimension it solves every run of the three branch problems. With niches set on the flat versions too, conditions still help at 50 and 1,000 evaluations per dimension (×0.09 and ×0.23) but not at 100 (×3.1), where layers-7 decides it: its runs either find three layers or settle on two or four, which costs 0.5, so its median flips between budgets.
  • CMA-ES and random search come out the same with conditions as without: they draw the same points, and an objective that ignores the parameters switched off sees the same values.
  • choose_optimizer's rule holds without change. Its pick is 1.15 times the best optimizer's error on geometric mean over all eight problems, and 1.07 times over the four with conditions.

The machine learning suite has a conditional problem too: model-selection-breast-cancer, choosing a support vector classifier, a random forest or k nearest neighbours and that model's settings (see Machine learning tuning).

docs.title: Constrained problems
docs.text:
python -m hone.benchmarks --constrained runs ten problems whose optimum lies on a constraint's boundary, as it usually does in engineering, at the same five budgets:

Problem What it tests boundary-sphere and boundary-ellipsoid, in 2, 5 and 10 dimensions A linear constraint that cuts off the unconstrained optimum, so the answer is on the cutting plane; the optimum is known exactly rosenbrock-disk-2d Rosenbrock's curved valley inside the disk x² + y² ≤ 2, with the optimum (1, 1) on the disk's edge pressure-vessel A vessel of least cost holding at least 1,296,000 cubic inches, with plate thicknesses in sixteenths of an inch: integers and three constraints tension-spring A spring of least weight under four limits; only 0.8% of the box satisfies them all welded-beam A welded beam of least cost under six limits, two of them functions with square roots; 2.9% of the box is feasible

The engineering problems are scored against the best designs published for them. Every optimizer only ever asks for feasible points, so each evaluation counts.

  • Bayesian optimization is the best at small budgets, more clearly than without constraints: it has the lowest median error on all ten problems at 10 and 20 evaluations per dimension, and all six it runs on at 50. On the pressure vessel with 40 evaluations its median cost is 266 above the best known design, against 10,010 for CMA-ES and 19,140 for random search.
  • CMA-ES is the best at 1,000 evaluations per dimension, on all ten problems. It finds the best known design of nine of them in every run, and of the pressure vessel in three of ten. When a candidate breaks a constraint, it draws again from the same distribution. Ranking such candidates below every feasible one without evaluating them was also tried, and did worse at every budget (×1.17 to ×1.59).
  • The genetic optimizer is behind CMA-ES under constraints, but it is the optimizer for constrained problems with choice or integer parameters, which CMA-ES can't search or handles less well. A child that breaks a constraint is moved back toward its fitter parent, halving the gap ten times, so it lands near the boundary. Against breeding a new child instead, this cut its geometric-mean error to ×0.84, ×0.68, ×0.74, ×0.46 and ×0.44 at 10 to 1,000 evaluations per dimension; on the welded beam at 1,000 it went from 0.080 to 0.0058. It beats random search on every problem at 50 and 1,000 evaluations per dimension, and on nine of ten at 100, losing on rosenbrock-disk-2d.
  • choose_optimizer's rule holds without change. Its pick is 1.04 times the best optimizer's error on geometric mean, and the best on 45 of the 50 problem and budget pairs.

docs.title: Multi-objective problems
docs.text:
python -m hone.benchmarks --multi runs seven problems with two or three objectives, at the same five budgets. A run is scored by the hypervolume gap: the true front's hypervolume less that of the front the run found, with each objective scaled from 0 at the true front's best value to 1 at its worst and a reference point of 1.1. 0 is the true front; lower is better. The scale is fixed per problem, so gaps compare across optimizers and seeds.

Problem What it tests zdt1-8d A convex front, with seven variables that must all be found to reach it rotated-zdt1-8d The same, with those seven variables turned by a fixed rotation so they interact zdt2-8d A concave front, which no weighted sum of the objectives can reach the middle of zdt3-8d A front in five separate pieces zdt4-6d Many false fronts, from a Rastrigin grid in five of the variables dtlz2-7d Three objectives, with a spherical front welded-beam-2 The welded beam's cost against its deflection, under its constraints; scored against the combined front of three NSGA2 runs of 50,000 evaluations

The ZDT and DTLZ2 problems are shifted so their best designs lie inside the bounds rather than on them, where clipping would find them for free. Weighted sums are the baseline, the usual way of getting a front without a multi-objective optimizer: the budget is shared among single-objective runs, each minimizing a weighted sum of the objectives (5 evenly spread weightings for two objectives, 6 for three), by the optimizer choose_optimizer would pick for its share. The objectives are scaled by the true front before weighting, which a real user couldn't do, so this baseline is generous.

  • Bayesian optimization with ParEGO is the best at small budgets. At 10 evaluations per dimension it has the lowest median gap on all six problems that any optimizer gets a front on, and at 20 Bayesian optimization, with one method or the other, does on five of six; on ZDT1 with 80 evaluations its gap is 0.16, against 0.33 for NSGA2 and 0.58 for weighted sums. It isn't run above 200 evaluations, where choosing each candidate takes longer than most evaluations it would save.
  • One model per objective (method="models") is the better choice for three objectives. On DTLZ2 at 20 evaluations per dimension its gap is 0.13 against ParEGO's 0.23, and on the welded beam the two are level. On the ZDT problems it is well behind ParEGO, so ParEGO is the default. A smoother estimate of its expected improvement was tried and made no difference.
  • NSGA2 is the best from 100 evaluations per dimension, on every problem but the welded beam at 100. At 1,000 its median gap is about 0.001 on all four ZDT problems, rotated or not, ten times closer than weighted sums, and 0.004 on the welded beam. It is the only optimizer to get onto ZDT4's front, at 1,000 evaluations per dimension.
  • Weighted sums hold up at 50 to 100 evaluations per dimension, ahead of NSGA2 on ZDT1, ZDT2 and the welded beam at 50. Past that they stall: on the concave ZDT2 at 1,000 their gap is 0.034 against NSGA2's 0.0013, since each weighting can only find an end of that front.
  • ZDT4 is out of reach at small budgets. Every optimizer's gap is 0.877, the whole hypervolume, until NSGA2 at 1,000 evaluations per dimension: no front lands inside the reference point before then.
  • choose_pareto_optimizer's rule holds. Where both run, ParEGO's median gap beats NSGA2's on 12 of the 13 problem and budget pairs they don't tie on, and a test checks the saved results still say so.

docs.title: Noisy problems
docs.text:
python -m hone.benchmarks --noisy adds Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 1 to every evaluation of six 5-dimensional problems: sphere, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin, rotated Ackley, mixed Rastrigin and material selection. Near their optima these problems' values differ by less than that, so the noise hides the differences an optimizer has to find. Every optimizer runs with noise=True, and each run is scored by the true, noise-free value of the point it returns, so a lucky result doesn't count. The noise is repeatable for each seed.

  • Bayesian optimization is best at small budgets: it has the lowest median error on all six problems at 10 evaluations per dimension, and on noisy-sphere-5d its median error is 0.44 against 3.3 for CMA-ES.
  • At 200 evaluations per dimension, the genetic optimizer has the most wins, five problems against one for CMA-ES.

docs.title: What noise=True does, measured
docs.text:
Each design choice was compared with and without it on these problems, over 10 seeds, as the ratio of geometric-mean errors:

Change 10 / dim 40 / dim 200 / dim Genetic optimizer: averaging, with parents ranked by their latest average ×1.01 ×0.92 ×0.74 Bayesian optimization: improvement measured against the model's best prediction ×0.95 ×0.90 not run CMA-ES: 10% of the budget kept back for a final round ×1.12 ×1.14 ×0.89 Random search: the same ×1.02 ×1.02 ×0.98

Some ideas that sound right made things worse, and were left out:

  • Re-evaluating the genetic optimizer's elites every generation cost evaluations and gave up most of the gain from averaging (×1.08, ×0.99 and ×1.04).
  • Telling Bayesian optimization's model to expect noise, through a prior on the noise level, made it worse than no noise handling at all (×1.13 and ×1.40); the model learns the noise from the data well enough.
  • Choosing Bayesian optimization's result by the model's prediction rather than by the averages was also worse than no noise handling (×1.13 at both budgets).
  • The final round costs more search than it gains until errors approach the noise level, which is why it is off by default.
